opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly my views on it have evolved since we first put out Mamba.

When we were developing it, the central insight was that earlier state space models like S4 were linear time-invariant. The dynamics governing how the hidden state evolves were the same at every timestep, regardless of the input. That gives you nice properties. You can compute the whole thing as a convolution, train it really efficiently, and it handles very long-range dependencies on things like audio or certain kinds of time series. But it also means the model can't decide what to remember and what to throw away based on the content it's seeing. And for discrete, information-dense data like language, that turns out to matter a lot. Tasks like selective copying or associative recall, where you have to pick out specific tokens and ignore filler, are hard for an LTI model.

So selectivity, making parameters like the step size and the input and output projections functions of the input, was really about giving the model that ability to filter. The step size in particular has a nice interpretation. A large step means "reset and focus on this current input," and a small step means "ignore this and keep my state." It's a generalization of the gating you see in classical RNNs like LSTMs and GRUs, and connecting it back to that lineage was part of the motivation.

Now, how important is the *particular* mechanism? I'd separate the principle from the specific parameterization. The principle, that the recurrence should be input-dependent so the state can be content-aware, I think is pretty fundamental. Most of the strong recurrent models that came after, whether gated linear attention variants, the various delta-rule models, or our own Mamba-2 work, have some form of data-dependent gating or decay. The field has largely converged on that.

The exact form, though, is much more flexible than people sometimes assume. In Mamba-2 we actually simplified things, restricting the state transition to a scalar times identity per head, and it worked about as well while being much more hardware-friendly. That told us a lot of the original structure wasn't strictly necessary. Then there's a whole design space beyond simple decay, like delta-rule-style updates, where you're not just decaying the state but actively overwriting specific associations. Those seem to help on recall-heavy tasks. So I see the original selection mechanism as one point in a bigger space, and there's still a lot to understand about which choices matter for which kinds of data.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that selectivity doesn't make a fixed-size state infinitely powerful. You're still compressing the whole history into a finite state. Selectivity lets you compress more intelligently, but there's a real trade-off against attention, which keeps everything around in a cache. That's part of why hybrids, mostly recurrent layers with a few attention layers, work so well in practice. Selectivity is what makes the recurrent layers good enough that you only need a little attention, rather than being a full replacement on its own.

So in short, I think selectivity was the key conceptual unlock that made these models competitive on language. But I wouldn't be dogmatic about the specific equations. The deeper lesson is about how to build models that compress context in a content-aware, efficient way, and we're still learning the best ways to do that.

r001.rationale: The response explains that input-dependent step sizes and projections determine whether new input resets or updates the recurrent state, or is ignored.

r002.rationale: It says Mamba-2’s simplified transition worked about as well and that recent models use forms of data-dependent gating or decay, but does not communicate the criterion’s state-expansion aspect or a broad comparison of models incorporating both selectivity and state expansion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think selectivity is really the crux of the whole thing, and it's worth being precise about what we mean by it. If you go back to the earlier structured state space models, S4 and that whole line of work, the recurrence was linear time-invariant. The transition matrices, the A and B and C, were fixed across the sequence. That gave you some really nice properties: you could compute the whole thing as a convolution, it was very efficient, and it was great for things like long-range signal processing, audio, that kind of continuous data. But it had a fundamental weakness on language-like data, because the model couldn't decide what to pay attention to. Every token got written into the state in exactly the same way, and every token decayed out of the state in exactly the same way. There was no content-dependent control.

The selectivity mechanism in Mamba is just the observation that if you let those parameters be functions of the input, so the step size, the input projection, the output projection all depend on the current token, then the recurrence becomes a sort of gating or filtering mechanism. The model can look at a token and say, this is important, let it in, open the gate, or this is filler, ignore it, keep the state as it is. And it can also decide how much to forget. If you think about it, that's exactly what you need for things like selective copying, or induction heads, or the kinds of in-context retrieval behaviors that attention does well and that time-invariant models just couldn't do.

Now, as far as the particular form of it, I'd say two things. One is that the specific parameterization matters less than people might think. We've seen a lot of variants since then, gated linear attention, RWKV, the various linear RNNs with data-dependent decay, and they all converge on this same core idea: you need an input-dependent forget gate, essentially, and an input-dependent write. The exact way you parameterize that, whether it's through a discretization step like we did, or a more direct gating formulation, those are details that affect things like stability and how easy it is to train, but the conceptual ingredient is the same. Honestly, I think that convergence is the most interesting signal. Lots of groups coming from very different starting points, whether that's RNNs, attention, or control theory, all arrived at roughly the same mechanism, and that tells you it's something fundamental about compressing a sequence into a fixed-size state.

The second thing I'd say is that selectivity is really about a tradeoff. Attention doesn't have to be selective, because it just keeps everything around in the KV cache and looks it up later. The cost is that the state grows with the sequence. A recurrent model has a fixed-size state, so it's forced to compress, and selectivity is the mechanism by which it decides what to compress. So it's not just an efficiency trick, it's actually a statement about what kind of inductive bias you're building in. And I think that's where the ongoing research is: understanding what these models can and can't hold in state, and where you want to combine them with attention layers in a hybrid to get the best of both.

r001.rationale: The response describes input-dependent writes, forgetting, and gating as determining what enters or remains in the recurrent state.

r002.rationale: It says different models share a core selective mechanism, but does not state that models with state expansion perform broadly similarly.

astra-6.text:
I think the important thing is that the model can choose what to remember and what to ignore based on the input. If you have a fixed-size recurrent state, you’re compressing everything you’ve seen into that state, so you need some way to decide which information deserves space there.

The particular mechanism we use in Mamba is one way to do that. I wouldn’t necessarily claim that every detail of it is essential, or that it’s the only way to get good performance. There’s a broader design space of input-dependent updates and gating mechanisms. What matters is how effectively they let the model preserve relevant information and discard irrelevant information, while still allowing an efficient implementation.

So I’d distinguish the general idea of selectivity, which I think is very important, from the specific parameterization, where I think there’s still room to explore.

r001.rationale: The response says selectivity lets the model choose what to remember or ignore based on the input and describes input-dependent updates to its fixed-size recurrent state.

r002.rationale: The response discusses variation in selectivity mechanisms but does not judge that recent models with selectivity and state expansion perform broadly similarly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important thing is the ability to be selective, more than the particular mechanism we used. When you have a recurrent model, you’re compressing everything you’ve seen into a fixed-size state. So you need to decide what to put into that state, what to keep, and what to forget. Ideally, those decisions depend on the input, rather than being fixed ahead of time.

In Mamba, we have a particular way of making the state-space parameters input-dependent, but I wouldn’t claim that’s the only way, or necessarily the best way, to do it. Different gating mechanisms could accomplish something similar. The interesting questions are whether the mechanism gives the model enough control over its memory, whether it’s easy to train, and whether you can implement it efficiently. I’d separate that general principle of selectivity from the specific parameterization we happened to use.

r001.rationale: It says selectivity determines what input information enters, remains in, or is forgotten from the recurrent state.

r002.rationale: It discusses alternative selectivity mechanisms in general, but does not say that recent selective recurrent models with state expansion perform broadly similarly.
